title: A Batched Hartigan's $k$-Means Clustering
claim: Our batched variant needs about as few iterations as the sequential method, both well below the standard baseline across many datasets.
layout: 1 panel, grouped bar chart across 12 datasets, dashed baseline at 1
description: A single wide grouped bar chart. The x-axis lists 12 datasets: Letter, MAGIC Gamma, Sepsis, Shuttle, Superconductivity, aloi, cod-rna, connect-4, covtype, mnist, phishing and skin-nonskin. Each dataset has a red bar for Hartigan and a blue bar for Batched Hartigan. The y-axis is 'Iters. / Loyd iters.' and runs from 0 to about 1. A dashed gray horizontal line at 1 marks Lloyd's baseline. Every bar sits between about 0.5 and 0.67, so both methods use roughly half of Lloyd's iterations. The red and blue bars are nearly equal in height on every dataset. A legend in the top-left corner identifies the two colors. The eye goes first to the paired bars sitting well under the dashed line.
caption: Median iteration ratio relative to Lloyd across k values. Both Hartigan variants converge in roughly half the epochs. This shows one advantage of Hartigan’s method, and that our Batched variant maintains it in practice.
abstract: Hartigan's $k$-means algorithm has theoretical advantages over the standard Lloyd's variant, which has become synonymous with "$k$-means". Yet, Hartigan's algorithm is far slower in practice due to its inherently sequential calculations. We devise a Batched Hartigan's method that enables vectorized calculation by exploiting the triangle inequality to expose a set of parallel-safe updates and a smaller set of sequential updates. This makes Hartigan's method competitive with Lloyd's in execution speed for the first time.
